attributes.description: The virtuous prince of Ayodhyá and son of Dasharatha, who accepts 14 years of exile to honor his father's word.
Ráma's devoted wife who insists on accompanying him into the forest exile.
Ráma's loyal younger brother who accompanies him into exile, serving as his protector.
King of Ayodhyá and father of Ráma, Bharat, and LakshmaG, who dies of grief after Ráma's banishment.
One of Dasharatha's queens who schemes to place her son Bharat on the throne and sends Ráma to exile.
Ráma's mother and senior queen of Ayodhyá, who blesses Ráma before his departure into the forest.
Queen of Ayodhyá and mother of LakshmaG and Zatrughna, who blesses LakshmaG to serve Ráma faithfully.
Son of Kaikeyí and Dasharatha, absent at Rájagriha during Ráma's exile; refuses to assume the throne.
Youngest brother of Ráma, who remains with Bharat at Rájagriha during the exile.
The royal charioteer who conveys Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG out of Ayodhyá into exile.
The Nisháda chief and friend of Ráma who receives them at the Gangá bank and keeps watch over them.
The royal household priest and chief counselor who directs the envoys to summon Bharat from Rájagriha.
A revered hermit-sage whose hermitage at the confluence of Yamuná and Gangá (Prayag) Ráma visits during exile.
A renowned Bráhman sage who attends the assembly after Dasharatha's death.
A venerable sage who participates in the council of Bráhmans after the king's death.
An ancient revered sage present at the assembly of Bráhmans in Ayodhyá.
A glorious sage who participates in the royal assembly after Dasharatha's death.
An innocent young ascetic accidentally shot by Dasharatha while he was filling a water-pot at the Sarju river.
King of the Gods and lord of thunder, frequently invoked in blessings and comparisons throughout the verses.
The preserver of the universe, invoked in Kaushalya's blessing; Ráma is compared to his power.
The creator God of the universe, invoked as the originator of all beings and divine order.
God of death and ruler of the southern realm where departed spirits dwell.
The God of cosmic waters and moral order, invoked in blessings for Ráma's protection.
The God of rain, mentioned in the discourse on the necessity of a king for prosperous lands.
The God of wealth and giver of golden boons, invoked in Kaushalya's blessing.
A divine sage and messenger of the Gods who is renowned for eloquence and wisdom.
The preceptor of the Gods, invoked as a protective guide for Ráma during his exile.
The regent of the planet Venus, invoked for Ráma's protection in the forest.
The royal capital of Kosala, home of Ráma and Dasharatha, plunged into mourning after Ráma's exile.
The dense forest wilderness where Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG are exiled for fourteen years.
The holy river whose bank Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG cross at the start of the exile journey.
The river on whose bank Dasharatha accidentally shot the hermit's son, an event that cursed his fate.
The city of Bharat's maternal grandfather A[vapati, where Bharat and Zatrughna reside during the exile.
The sacred confluence of Gangá and Yamuná rivers, near Bharadvája's hermitage; modern Allahabad.
A sacred river whose waters blend with Gangá at Prayag, passed by Ráma during the forest journey.
The prosperous kingdom ruled by Dasharatha with Ayodhyá as its capital.
A flowering tree on the Gangá bank where Ráma halts and rests during the early stage of exile.
The 14-year banishment of Ráma to the DaGak forest, initiated by Kaikeyí's boon from Dasharatha.
The death of King Dasharatha from grief following Ráma's departure into exile.
The ceremonial blessing and rites performed by Queen Kaushalya for Ráma before his departure.
The formal leave-taking of Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG from Ayodhyá in Sumantra's chariot.
Sumantra's return to Ayodhyá alone after leaving Ráma at the forest, conveying Ráma's final message.
Dasharatha's accidental killing of a hermit's son on the Sarju bank while hunting by sound in his youth.
The council of Bráhmans and ministers who met after Dasharatha's death to decide on installing a king.
Vaishtha's dispatch of fast messengers to summon Bharat back to Ayodhyá after the king's death.
Ráma's first night halt under the Ingudí tree on the Gangá bank during the forest journey.
Ráma and LakshmaG's arrival at the sage Bharadvája's hermitage near Prayag during the exile journey.
The moral and cosmic duty or righteousness that governs Ráma's actions and choices throughout the narrative.
The obligation of a son to honor and obey his parents, central to Ráma's acceptance of exile.
The concept of righteous rule; the assembly's discourse highlights the necessity of a king for justice and prosperity.
The keeping of sworn words; Dasharatha's oath to Kaikeyí and Ráma's own pledge drive key events.
Banishment to the forest as a form of renunciation and testing, undertaken by Ráma for 14 years.
The sacred epic poem narrating the deeds of Ráma, authored by Válmíki.
A canto in which the Bráhmans lament the dangers of a kingless land after Dasharatha's death.
The canto in which Vaishtha sends swift messengers to bring Bharat back from Rájagriha.
The canto in which Dasharatha confesses to Kaushalya his past sin of accidentally killing a hermit's son.
The canto recording Queen Kaushalya's elaborate ritual blessing of Ráma before his departure into exile.
The canto where Sítá successfully persuades Ráma to allow her to accompany him into the forest.
The canto describing the formal departure of Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG from Ayodhyá.

entities.name: The Halt Under The Ingudí (Canto L)

attributes.description: The canto in which Ráma rests at the Gangá bank under the Ingudí tree and meets the Nisháda king Guha.
The canto in which LakshmaG laments the suffering caused by Ráma's exile while keeping night watch.
The canto describing Ráma's visit to the sage Bharadvája at the confluence of Gangá and Yamuná.

attributes.context: Ráma is described as embodying divine power comparable to VishGu throughout the epic.
Ráma is the eldest and most beloved son of King Dasharatha.
Ráma is the son of Queen Kaushalya who blesses him before exile.
Sítá is Ráma's devoted wife who accompanies him into exile.
LakshmaG is Ráma's younger brother and constant companion in exile.
Ráma is the prince of Ayodhyá who departs from and will eventually return to this city.
Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG spend 14 years in exile in the DaGak forest.
Ráma willingly accepts the 14-year exile to uphold his father's sworn word.
Ráma departs Ayodhyá in Sumantra's chariot with Sítá and LakshmaG.
Ráma halts under the Ingudí tree on the Gangá bank on the first night of exile.
Ráma visits sage Bharadvája at the confluence of Gangá and Yamuná.
Sítá insists on accompanying Ráma into the forest despite his objections.
Sítá departs Ayodhyá with Ráma in Sumantra's chariot.
Sítá accompanies Ráma into the DaGak forest during the exile.
LakshmaG voluntarily accompanies Ráma as his devoted protector during exile.
LakshmaG departs with Ráma and Sítá from Ayodhyá.
LakshmaG is the son of Queen Sumitrá, who blesses him to serve Ráma faithfully.
LakshmaG stands guard through the night at the Ingudí tree while Ráma sleeps.
Kaikeyí is one of Dasharatha's queens whose boon leads to Ráma's exile.
Kaushalya is Dasharatha's senior queen and mother of Ráma.
Dasharatha is the King of Ayodhyá who rules Ko[ala from this capital.
Dasharatha dies of grief after sending Ráma into exile.
Dasharatha accidentally killed the hermit's son on the Sarju bank in his youth while hunting by sound.
Dasharatha repeatedly speaks of Ráma in grief and love after the exile.
Kaikeyí demands Ráma's banishment as one of her two boons from Dasharatha.
Kaikeyí resides in the palace of Ayodhyá and schemes within its walls.
Kaushalya performs elaborate blessing rites for Ráma before his departure.
Kaushalya blesses Ráma and entreats him to take Sítá safely to the forest.
Kaushalya counsels Sítá on the duty of a devoted wife before departure.
Sumitrá instructs LakshmaG to treat Ráma as his lord and Sítá as his mother.
Sumantra drives the royal chariot carrying Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG out of Ayodhyá.
Sumantra returns alone to Ayodhyá bearing Ráma's parting messages.
Sumantra returns to Ayodhyá after leaving Ráma at the forest.
Guha, the Nisháda chief, comes to welcome Ráma at the Gangá bank and keeps night watch.
Guha is Ráma's dear friend of Nisháda lineage and sovereign lord of the Nisháda region.
Guha's kingdom lies along the Gangá bank near the Ingudí tree.
Vaishtha presides over the assembly of sages and ministers after the king's death.
Vaishtha orders the dispatch of fast messengers to summon Bharat.
Bharat stays in Rájagriha with his maternal grandfather during Ráma's exile.
Bharat is Ráma's younger brother by Kaikeyí who reveres Ráma and refuses the throne.
Zatrughna accompanies Bharat at Rájagriha during the exile period.
Bharadvája's hermitage is located near the confluence of Gangá and Yamuná at Prayag.
Bharadvája receives Ráma and LakshmaG at his hermitage near Prayag.
Nárad describes Ráma's divine virtues to Válmíki.
Indra is invoked in blessings comparing Ráma's victories to Indra's slaying of Vritra.
Dharma is the guiding principle behind all of Ráma's decisions including acceptance of exile.
Ráma's filial duty to obey his father drives his willingness to accept exile.
Dasharatha's sworn oath to Kaikeyí compels him to send Ráma into exile against his will.
The assembly debates the necessity of kingship for Ayodhyá's welfare after Dasharatha's death.
The Rámáyan is the sacred text that narrates all events of Ráma's life and exile.
This canto records the ritual blessing Kaushalya performs for Ráma before his departure.
This canto narrates how Sítá convinces Ráma to let her accompany him into the forest.
This canto records the formal leave-taking from Ayodhyá.

relationships.from: The Halt Under The Ingudí (Canto L)

attributes.context: This canto describes Ráma's first night halt at the Gangá bank.
This canto captures LakshmaG's emotional lament during the night watch at the Gangá bank.
This canto narrates Dasharatha's confession of accidentally killing the hermit's son.
This canto presents the Bráhmans' discourse on why a kingless land is doomed.
This canto records Vaishtha's dispatch of envoys to summon Bharat.
This canto describes Ráma's arrival at Bharadvája's hermitage near Prayag.
